extraction.note: Several of these are not model errors. PROJECT/period codes and numeric tokens are extracted with a low confidence and are not annotated as entities in the gold set, so they appear as false positives here.

interpretation.observation: TF-IDF + logistic regression scores higher than the rule baseline.
interpretation.explanation: The classifier memorised our own templates. The benign look-alikes reuse the same sentence frames as the attack records with a different middle clause, which is exactly the discrimination a bag-of-ngrams model is good at and a human is not fooled by. Treat the TF-IDF numbers as an upper bound that depends on the generator, not as evidence of generalisation.
interpretation.mitigation: The real public corpus is scored separately in risk_eval.json; that number is the one to trust about wording we did not write.

interpretation.observation: The rule baseline produces false positives on genuine urgent reminders.
interpretation.explanation: 'your account will be closed' and 'immediately' both appear in legitimate bank reminders. The mitigator list catches some of these and not all of them: a reminder that omits the 'no charge' sentence loses its mitigation.
interpretation.mitigation: The API reports each indicator separately with its evidence, so a user can see that the flag came from a policy sentence rather than a demand. Severity only reaches 'warning' when a payment demand is paired with a threat or a deadline.

embedding_backend.note: Real sentence-transformer embeddings, computed locally on CPU.

interpretation.explanation: Most queries in this benchmark are entity names lifted from the record, which is the strongest possible case for exact lexical matching and the weakest possible case for embeddings. Fusing a weaker channel with equal weight therefore costs recall on this corpus.
interpretation.mitigation: The per-kind breakdown shows where fusion does help. Keep the two channels separately selectable in Settings, and let the paraphrase queries - where BM25 has no lexical overlap at all - be the reason hybrid is the default.

interpretation.explanation: The right record is usually found, but several records are equally relevant so the first position is nearly a coin flip. Binary relevance makes nDCG look poor for the same reason.
interpretation.mitigation: Treat MRR as the meaningful number for topical queries and Recall@k for 'which records mention X'. Both are reported.

caveats: Relevance is binary: a record is relevant or it is not. This suits 'which records mention X' and understates topical queries.
Queries are derived from the same generator that wrote the records, so the corpus is easier than real user data would be.
nDCG uses the same binary gains as Recall, so it mostly re-orders the Recall numbers rather than adding an independent view.

interpretation.observation: Recall is lower than precision: P=1.000 vs R=0.739.
interpretation.explanation: The resolver is deliberately conservative. A missed merge leaves two entities the user can inspect; a wrong merge silently asserts that two different people are the same, which is the more damaging error in a graph the user is meant to trust.
interpretation.mitigation: Clusters below the cohesion threshold are reported to the user as possibly-merged rather than being merged silently.

interpretation: The projection onto our indicators is deliberately conservative: only 'urgency' survives on real spam text. Real SMS spam rarely makes an explicit threat or an explicit emotional appeal - it relies on scarcity and a prize instead.

That is a genuine finding, not a bug. It means our four indicators cover the long-form business-email manipulation in Scenario A far better than they cover consumer SMS fraud, and the report should not claim otherwise.
